entry: Surface of points all lying at the same distance from a fixed center point. In solid geometry, a sphere is the set of points in [[Three-dimensional space|three-dimensional space]] that are all the same distance, the radius, from a given point. It is the three-dimensional analogue of a [[Circle]]. Spheres are fundamental in [[Mathematics]], and they occur in nature and industry: soap bubbles take a spherical shape in equilibrium, and pressure vessels and most curved mirrors and lenses are based on spheres. The Earth is often approximated as a sphere in [[Geography]], and the celestial sphere is central to [[Astronomy]]. Spheres roll smoothly in any direction, so most sports balls, toys and ball bearings are spherical. Mathematicians distinguish the sphere, a two-dimensional closed surface, from the solid ball it encloses.

System that locates a point in three-dimensional space by a distance and two angles. The coordinates are the radial distance r from a fixed origin, the polar angle θ between the radial line and a given polar axis, and the azimuthal angle φ, the rotation of the radial line around that axis. Once the radius is fixed, the three coordinates provide a coordinate system on a [[Sphere|sphere]]. Naming order and symbols differ among disciplines, and mathematics texts often swap the two angles. Mathematical systems normally measure angles in [[Radian|radians]] rather than degrees.

Special functions defined on the surface of a [[Sphere|sphere]]. They are often used in solving [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] in many scientific fields. Because they form a complete orthogonal set, a function on a sphere can be written as a sum of them, much as a periodic function can be expanded in [[Fourier series]]. They originate from solutions to [[Laplace's equation]], and [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Pierre Simon de Laplace]] first introduced them in 1782. Their applications include electromagnetic fields, [[Electron configuration|electron configurations]], gravitational fields, geoids and the [[Cosmic microwave background]]. In 3D computer graphics they model indirect lighting.

Mythical creature with a lion's body and a human head, found in Egyptian and Greek tradition. In Greek tradition the sphinx is a treacherous being with a woman's head, a lion's haunches and a bird's wings. She challenges travelers with a riddle and kills those who fail to answer, a version that appears in the myth and drama of [[Oedipus]]. In Egyptian mythology the sphinx is typically depicted as a man, usually representing a [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]]'s strength and ferocity, and it was not winged. Both traditions cast sphinxes as guardians, and statues often flank the entrances to temples. The most famous is the [[Great Sphinx of Giza]], on the [[Giza]] Plateau near the Great Pyramids. Egyptologists consider its head to bear the likeness of the pharaoh Khafre, dating it to between 2600 and 2500 BC. The sphinx enjoyed a major revival in European decorative art during the [[Renaissance]].

Hairless breed of [[Cat|cat]], also known as the Canadian Sphynx. Hairlessness in cats is a naturally occurring genetic mutation, and breeders developed the Sphynx through [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]] starting in the 1960s. Its skin has the texture of chamois leather and may bear fine hairs or none. Because these cats lose body heat more readily than coated cats, they are warm to the touch and seek out warm places. The breed began in 1966 in [[Toronto]], [[Ontario]], when a hairless male kitten was born to a domestic shorthair. Sphynx cats have wedge-shaped heads, large eyes and ears.

English girl group formed in 1994. Its members were Mel B, Melanie C, Emma Bunton, Geri Halliwell and Victoria Beckham, known as Scary, Sporty, Baby, Ginger and Posh Spice. With the slogan "girl power," the group targeted a young female audience and led the teen pop resurgence of the 1990s. Its debut album, *Spice* (1996), sold more than 23 million copies, and the 1998 Spiceworld Tour was the highest-grossing concert tour by a female group. The group entered a hiatus in 2000 and has since reunited for tours. It has sold more than 110 million records worldwide.

Fictional [[Superhero|superhero]] in American comic books published by [[Marvel Comics]]. Created by writer-editor [[Stan Lee]] and artist Steve Ditko, Spider-Man first appeared in *Amazing Fantasy* #15 in August 1962, during the Silver Age of comic books. Peter Benjamin Parker, raised by his aunt and uncle in [[Queens]], [[New York City]], gains spider-like powers after being bitten by a radioactive spider. After his uncle is killed by a burglar he could have helped capture, he learns that "with great power comes great responsibility" and fights crime as Spider-Man. The character has appeared in comic books, television, films and video games. Live-action films have featured Tobey Maguire, Andrew Garfield and Tom Holland, and Marvel has published alternate versions, including Miles Morales, the teenage hero of *Ultimate Comics: Spider-Man*.

Order of air-breathing [[Arthropod|arthropods]] with eight limbs and silk-producing spinnerets. Spiders (order *Araneae*) are the largest order of [[Arachnid|arachnids]] and are found worldwide on every continent except Antarctica. As of January 2026, 53,680 spider species in 139 families had been recorded. Unlike [[Insect|insects]], spiders have no antennae, and their fanged chelicerae generally inject [[Venom|venom]]. Spider [[Silk|silk]] combines lightness, strength and elasticity superior to synthetic materials. Nearly all species are predators, mostly of insects and other spiders. Females of many species care for their young, and most spiders live for at most two years, while [[Tarantula|tarantulas]] can live for over 20 years. Scientists are studying spider venom for use in medicine and as non-polluting pesticides.

Genus of [[New World monkey|New World monkeys]] with long limbs and a prehensile tail. Spider monkeys, genus *Ateles*, live in the [[Rainforest|rainforests]] of Central and South America, from southern [[Mexico]] to [[Brazil]], where they forage in the high canopy. They lack thumbs and are among the largest New World monkeys. They are so called because they hang from branches by their tails, with their long limbs suspended like spiders dangling from a web. They mainly eat fruit and live in bands of up to 35 individuals. Meta-analyses of primate cognition studies from the 2000s indicated they are the most intelligent New World monkeys. All species are threatened, and the brown spider monkey is critically endangered.

American filmmaker and actor. His films explore race relations, issues within the black community, the role of media in contemporary life, and urban crime and poverty. Lee studied at [[New York University]]'s Tisch School of the Arts and made his directing debut with *She's Gotta Have It* (1986). *Do the Right Thing* (1989) earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Screenplay, and *BlacKkKlansman* (2018) won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay. He directed the [[HBO]] series *When the Levees Broke* (2006), which won two Primetime Emmy Awards.

Intrinsic form of [[Angular momentum|angular momentum]] carried by elementary particles, atomic nuclei and atoms. Spin is quantized, so it takes only discrete values, and accurate models of its interaction require relativistic [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] or [[Quantum field theory|quantum field theory]]. The existence of electron spin was inferred from the Stern–Gerlach experiment, in which silver atoms showed two possible discrete angular momenta despite having no orbital angular momentum. The relativistic spin–statistics theorem connects spin to the [[Pauli exclusion principle|Pauli exclusion principle]]: particles that obey exclusion have half-integer spin, and half-integer spin implies exclusion. Spin is described mathematically as a vector for particles such as [[Photon|photons]] and as a spinor for particles such as electrons. In practice, spin is given as a dimensionless spin quantum number, found by dividing the spin angular momentum by the reduced [[Planck constant]] ħ.

Annual leafy green [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]], *Spinacia oleracea*, native to Central and Western Asia. Its leaves are a common vegetable, eaten fresh, cooked or preserved by [[Canning|canning]], freezing or dehydration. Blanching may reduce its high oxalate content. Raw spinach is 91% water and a rich source of vitamin A, [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]], manganese and folate, with an especially high content of vitamin K. The [[Arabs]] introduced spinach to [[Sicily]] in 827 CE, and it first appeared in England and France in the 14th century. It is mentioned in the first known English cookbook, the *Forme of Cury* (1390). In 2024, world production was 31 million tonnes, with China accounting for 92% of the total.

Segmented column of bone that forms the core of the axial skeleton in [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]]. Also called the vertebral column, spine or backbone, it surrounds and protects the [[Spinal cord|spinal cord]], and its vertebrae are separated by intervertebral discs. Around 50,000 species of animals have a vertebral column. In humans there are normally 33 vertebrae: seven cervical, twelve thoracic and five lumbar, with the lower nine fused in adults, five in the sacrum and four in the coccyx. The total ranges from 32 to 35. The atlas and axis support the head. Clinical landmarks on vertebrae guide [[Lumbar puncture|lumbar punctures]] and spinal anesthesia. Spina bifida is the most common birth defect affecting the spinal column.

Long, thin tubular structure of nervous tissue in the backbone of vertebrates. It extends from the medulla oblongata in the lower [[Brainstem|brainstem]] to the lumbar region of the vertebral column, and with the [[Brain|brain]] it makes up the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]]. Its center is hollow and contains a central canal filled with cerebrospinal fluid. It is about 45 cm (18 in) long in adult men and 43 cm (17 in) in adult women. The cord carries nerve signals between the brain and the body, and it coordinates many [[Reflex|reflexes]]. Groups of [[Neuron|neurons]] form circuits that control rhythmic movements such as walking. Its diameter ranges from 13 mm (1⁄2 in) in the cervical and lumbar regions to 6.4 mm (1⁄4 in) in the thoracic area.

Magnesium aluminum oxide mineral, MgAl₂O₄, also used as a [[Gemstone|gemstone]]. Its name comes from the Latin *spinella*, a diminutive of *spine*, for its pointed crystals. It is found in metamorphosed [[Limestone|limestone]] and in some rare igneous rocks. Its hardness is 8, and it ranges from colorless to red, lavender, blue, green, brown, black and yellow. Chromium causes the red color of spinel from [[Myanmar]]. Some famous gemstones are spinels, including the Black Prince's Ruby and the Timur Ruby in the British Crown Jewels. The Samarian Spinel, the largest known spinel, weighs 500 carats (100 g).

Toy with a squat round body that tapers to a point, designed to be spun on its vertical axis. A spinning top balances on its tip because of the gyroscopic effect, which stabilizes its rotation against gravity. Tops are made of wood, metal or plastic and include peg-tops and whip-tops. Once spinning, a top wobbles briefly, then spins upright for a time that depends on speed and friction, before tipping over. Tops are among the oldest known toys, found by archaeologists on every inhabited continent. Clay tops from [[Mesopotamia]] date back about 5,000 years, and tops were used as toys in [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]] and [[Ancient Greece|Greece]]. The teetotum, a four-sided gambling top, was later adapted into the dreidel, a Jewish toy played during [[Hanukkah]].

Genus of large spinosaurid [[Theropoda|theropod]] dinosaurs It lived about 100 to 94 million years ago in the [[Cretaceous]] period. The first remains, from Egypt, were discovered in 1912 and described by Ernst Stromer in 1915. The originals were destroyed in [[World War II]], but later finds came from Morocco and Niger. Its long neural spines formed a sail-like structure, and its skull was long, low and narrow, similar to that of a modern crocodilian. A 2022 study suggests that *S. aegyptiacus* could have reached 14 m (46 ft) in length and 7.4 t (8.2 short tons) in body mass.

Class of [[Galaxy|galaxy]] whose flat, rotating disk has spiral arms extending from its center. [[Edwin Hubble]] described the class in his 1936 work *The Realm of the Nebulae*, and spiral galaxies form part of the Hubble sequence. Most have a flat disk of stars, gas and dust, a central bulge of stars and a fainter halo, many of whose stars reside in globular clusters. The spiral arms are sites of ongoing star formation and appear brighter than the disk because of young, hot OB stars. Roughly two-thirds have a bar-like structure extending from the bulge. The [[Milky Way]] is a barred spiral. Many bulges host a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] at their center. Together with irregular galaxies, spiral galaxies make up approximately 60% of galaxies in today's universe.

2001 Japanese animated fantasy film by [[Hayao Miyazaki]], produced by [[Studio Ghibli]]. It follows ten-year-old Chihiro Ogino, who enters a world of kami, the spirits of Japanese [[Shinto]] folklore, after her parents are turned into pigs by the witch Yubaba. She takes a job in Yubaba's bathhouse to free her parents and return to the human world. Distributed in Japan by [[Toho]], the film was released on July 20, 2001, with a budget of US$19 million. It grossed ¥31.68 billion in Japan, the highest-grossing film in Japanese history until 2020, and US$396 million worldwide. It won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature at the 75th Academy Awards, the first hand-drawn, non-English-language animated film to do so.

Type of domestic dog including between 50 and 70 breeds. Most spitz breeds have pricked ears, almond-shaped eyes, a pointed muzzle, a double coat and a tail that curves over the back. The name derives from the German *Spitz(hund)*, meaning "pointed (dog)," after the muzzle. Most originate from the [[Arctic]] or [[Siberia]]. Thick undercoats and small upright ears help them survive harsh northern climates. Many breeds, such as the [[Chow Chow]] and the Japanese Akita, keep [[Wolf|wolf]]-like independence and need much socialization as puppies. Huskies were bred for one purpose only, while the tiny Pomeranian was bred down from a much larger dog into a companion.

Organ found in almost all [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] that acts primarily as a blood filter. Similar in structure to a large lymph node, it lies near the [[Liver|liver]]. It removes old [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]] and holds a reserve of blood that can be valuable in cases of hemorrhagic shock. It also recycles iron from hemoglobin, and its heme portion is metabolized to bilirubin, which is removed in the liver. The white pulp houses T and B lymphocytes that help produce [[Antibody|antibodies]], giving the spleen a role in the [[Immune system|immune system]]. The red pulp filters blood and stores monocytes that can travel to sites of tissue injury. In humans the spleen is purple and lies in the left upper abdomen. Surgical removal is called splenectomy.

Second-largest city in [[Croatia]], on the eastern shore of the [[Adriatic Sea]]. Founded as a Greek colony, it developed around the palace of the Roman emperor [[Diocletian]], which became a palace site in 305 CE. The city has a population of over 160,000. It later came under the [[Republic of Venice|Republic of Venice]], then the Austrian Empire, and then [[Yugoslavia]] after 1918. Its historic core is a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site, and the city attracts over one million visitors annually.

Fictional science officer in the [[Star Trek]] media franchise. Spock served as first officer and science officer of the starship *Enterprise* in the original [[Star Trek: The Original Series|Star Trek series]] (1966–69), alongside Captain James T. Kirk and Dr. Leonard McCoy. [[Leonard Nimoy|Leonard Nimoy]] played him in the original series and eight Star Trek feature films, and his portrayal earned him three Emmy Award nominations. Spock's mixed human-Vulcan heritage is an important plot element. Ethan Peck has played an earlier Spock, and Zachary Quinto played an alternate-reality Spock in three films.

City (pop., 2020: 228,989), county seat of Spokane County in eastern [[Washington (state)|Washington]]. It lies along the Spokane River, about 280 miles (450 km) east of [[Seattle]]. The city was incorporated as Spokane Falls in 1881 and adopted its current name ten years later. Architect Kirtland Cutter designed many downtown buildings after the Great Spokane Fire of 1889. Gonzaga University was established by the [[Jesuits]] in 1887. The city hosted Expo '74, the first environmentally themed [[World's fair]]. It is known as the birthplace of Father's Day.

American animated comedy television series for [[Nickelodeon]]. Created by marine science educator Stephen Hillenburg, it follows an anthropomorphic yellow [[Sponge|sea sponge]] and his aquatic friends in the underwater city of Bikini Bottom. It premiered on July 17, 1999, after a sneak peek on May 1, 1999. Critics have praised its surreal humor and writing, and it is often considered one of the greatest animated series of all time. It has won four Emmy Awards and a record 23 Kids' Choice Awards. The show is a cultural touchstone for [[Millennials]] and [[Generation Z]] and has spawned numerous [[Internet meme|internet memes]].
